newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - S.African sugar companies cut into Africa.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - S.African sugar companies cut into Africa.

text.p: South African sugar companies, hungry for growth, are cutting paths deeper into the African sugar industry.

The country's largest sugar firm, Illovo Sugar Ltd last month bought the sugar division of Lonrho Plc -- which includes interests in Mauritius, Malawi and Swaziland -- for 1.6 billion rand ($356 million).
Tongaat-Hulett Group Ltd said recently it would expand into Zimbabwe and build a 260 million rand sugar mill with a capacity of around 140,000 tonnes a year.

"We are seeing this move towards a regional market and the various South African companies are in the race to secure their positions in the wider regional market," Investec Securities analyst Carolyn Windsor said.
EXPANSION INTO UGANDA, TANZANIA SEEN
Windsor said she expected Tongaat-Hulett to forge firmer ties with Britain's Tate & Lyle Plc and also seek to expand into Uganda and Tanzania.
"Any development or expansion that we see coming from Tongaat appears to me that it is going to be done very much in conjunction with Tate."
Tongaat and Tate already have a good working relationship and submitted a joint bid for Lonrho Sugar. They have also formed joint ventures in Namibia and Botswana.
Windsor said some sugar estates in Tanzania and Uganda were up for privatisation which could attract Tongaat.
Both Illovo and Tongaat favoured expansion into low-cost producing areas and southern Africa was one of the lowest-cost production areas in the world.
Illovo's purchase of Lonrho's sugar business created Africa's largest sugar group with interests in southern and East Africa.

"The acquisition of Lonrho Sugar is an extremely exciting development for Illovo and is consistent with our stated strategy to focus on sugar, downstream products and expansion into sub-Saharan Africa," Illovo managing director Don MacLeod said.
ILLOVO SEEN CONSOLIDATING POSITION
Analysts said they expected Illovo to consolidate its position as the leading sugar company in southern Africa after the Lonrho deal.
"Illovo will be consolidating its position, I don't think you are going to see much more further activity into Africa from them whilst they are busy digesting the Lonsugar acquisition," Windsor said.
Illovo owns seven sugar mills in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province and this year expanded into Mozambique and Kenya.

It also submitted a bid to buy the Ivory Coast's state-owned sugar company Sodesucre but seems to have been pipped by Britain's ED&F Man which submitted the highest bid. The final result of the tender is not yet known.

Although South Africa is the biggest sugar producer on the continent with a huge domestic market consuming around 1.3 million tonnes of sugar a year, most of its southern African neighbours produce sugar at a lower cost.
SOUTH AFRICAN MARKET REMAINS IMPORTANT

"We are not looking at the demise of the South African market at all. South Africa still is going to be the most important market both in terms of production and consumption. It is obviously the largest market and the richest market," Windsor said.
South Africa produced a 1997/98 (April-March) sugar crop of 2.5 million tonnes of sugar -- which will leave 1.2 million tonnes for export after lucrative domestic market needs have been met.

South Africa's sugar industry dwarfs that of its neighbours. In recent months the usually cordial relations between the industry and its neigbours have been soured through a bitter dispute with tiny Swaziland.

Last year, the South African Sugar Association (SASA) cut all ties with Swaziland and withdrew research and training facilities from the Swazis after accusing the mountain kingdom's industry of dumping its much cheaper sugar on the South African domestic market.
